newsitem.title: USA: Wall St stocks weak at midday, mergers dominate.
newsitem.headline: Wall St stocks weak at midday, mergers dominate.

text.p: U.S. stocks were weak at midday Tuesday as the market consolidated after closing above 7,000 for the first time last week, and investors turned their attention to a burst of merger activity.
The Dow Industrials were down five at 6984 while declines and advances had a slightly negative bias.

"We're seeing consolidation after the big move. The focus has shifted to mergers and acquisitions which are dominating the tape today while the rest of the market takes a breather," said Oppenheimer & Co chief investment strategist Michael Metz.
The Dow drew strength from a rally in shares of Philip Morris Cos Inc -- up 3-1/4 at 128-3/4 and accounting for about nine points of Dow strength. The average later was up five points to 6994.
"The mergers are symptomatic of a slow-growth environment in which it is hard to get top-line earnings growth, so you get it from hollowing out the middle," Metz said.
"They allow restructuring to reduce expenses and improve earnings. They help the overall market because speculators search around for possible next targets and bid them up."

Great Western Financial Corp was up 9-3/8 at 43-5/8, topping the NYSE most active list, after H.F. Ahmanson and Co said it was offering $42.53 a share for Great Western. Ahmanson shares were up 3-3/4 at 44-14.
Renaissance Hotel Group N.V. shares were up 4-1/2 at 29-5/8 after Marriott International Inc said it agreed to acquire Renaissance for $30 per share cash in a deal worth a total of $1 billion.
Horizon/CMS Healthcare Corp was up 2-3/8 at 16-5/8. Healthsouth Corp was down 1-3/4 at 41-3/8.
Healthsouth and Horizon said they had agreed to merge in a stock swap valued at about $1.6 billion.
But analysts said that aside from the interest in mergers, market players were likely to take it easy today and wait for tomorrow's January consumer price index to give them some guidance.

"I have the impression that traders and portfolio managers are shaking out the cobwebs after the long weekend," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "We've all had a chance to see where we are and have reached the conclusion that we have come awfully far awfully fast."
He said that the stock market, as measured by the Dow Industrials, had risen 8.4 percent from the strat of the year through Friday.
"The chances of keeping this up are not good," Johnson said. "Investors have decided to pull in the reins and slow down a little bit."

The rally in shares of Philip Morris came after the company said that a West Virginia judge dismissed the "essential claims" of the state attorney general's Medicaid reimbursement lawsuit against tobacco companies.
